1.title: Container Images and Container Commands
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Container Images and Container Commands. It covers the exam area Application Design and Build. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. From a Docker file to a running container. Build, tag, run, save. Using an image in a Pod. Container commands: entry point, C M D, command and args. Practice with five hands-on labs worth twenty-seven points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Design and Build (twenty percent). Practice in this module: five labs, twenty-seven points, about twenty-nine minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: From a Dockerfile to a running container
1.text: From a Docker file to a running container. The figure shows this: The path of a container image.

1.title: From a Dockerfile to a running container, continued
1.text: From a Docker file to a running container. A container image is a read-only package: a file system plus the default command to run. You describe it in a Docker file, build it with a tool ( docker build or pod man build ), and either keep it on the machine, save it as a file, or push it to a registry. A Pod names the image; the kubelet on the node pulls it and starts the container.

1.title: The Dockerfile lines: building the image
1.text: The Docker file lines: building the image. from. What it does: the base image; always the first real line. Example: from busy box one dot thirty-six. run. What it does: run a command while building; makes a new layer. Example: run apk add the no cache flag curl. copy. What it does: copy files from the build folder into the image. Example: copy app dot conf slash E T C slash app dot conf. work dir. What it does: the working directory for later lines and for the container. Example: work dir slash app. environment. What it does: set an environment variable, kept at run time. Example: environment greeting hello. arg. What it does: a build-time variable, not kept at run time. Example: arg version one.

1.title: The Dockerfile lines: metadata and the start command
1.text: The Docker file lines: metadata and the start command. label. What it does: metadata on the image. Example: label version two. expose. What it does: documents the port the app listens on (does not publish it). Example: expose eighty eighty. user. What it does: the user the container runs as. Example: user one thousand. entry point. What it does: the program that always runs. Example: entry point echo. C M D. What it does: the default arguments, or the default command if there is no entry point. Example: C M D hello.

1.title: Layers, the build cache and multi-stage builds
1.text: Layers, the build cache and multi-stage builds. Layers and the build cache. Each run, copy and A D D line creates a layer. Docker reuses unchanged layers, so put the lines that change often (your code) at the bottom and the slow, stable ones (installing packages) at the top. Exec form versus shell form. C M D sleep, three thousand six hundred (a Jason array) starts the program directly. C M D sleep three thousand six hundred (a plain string) starts it through slash bin slash sh dash c. Use the exec form, and use a shell ( sh, dash c, echo greeting ) only when you need variable expansion. Multi-stage builds use several from lines: build in a large image, then copy the from flag set to build only the result into a small final image. The final image stays small and holds no compilers.

1.title: Build, tag, run, save
1.text: Build, tag, run, save. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Build, tag, run, save, continued
1.text: Build, tag, run, save. Build from another file name. docker build dash f Docker file dot prod dash t app two. Pass a build argument. docker build the build arg flag version two dash t app two. See the layers. docker history hello one dot zero. Read the labels and the command. docker image inspect hello one dot zero. Remove an image. docker rmi hello one dot zero. Exam tip: After a build, check the tag with docker images; save an image with docker save name tag file dot tar, and pod man uses the same commands.

1.title: Build, tag, run, save, continued
1.text: Build, tag, run, save. Names. An image name is registry slash repository tag, for example registry dot K eights dot io slash pause three dot ten. Without a registry the default is Docker Hub. Without a tag the tag is latest, which is a name, not a promise of the newest build: always give a real tag.

1.title: Build, tag, run, save, continued
1.text: Build, tag, run, save. On the exam. The curriculum says "define, build and modify container images". The official pages read for this course do not say which tool is installed in the exam environment. Typical tasks edit a Docker file and build or save an image; if the tool is pod man, the commands above are identical with pod man instead of docker. Check which one exists ( which pod man docker ) and read the task for the tag and the output file.

1.title: Using an image in a Pod
1.text: Using an image in a Pod. A Pod references the image by name and tag. Two settings decide what the kubelet does. image. name tag, or name@S H A two fifty-six... to pin an exact build. image Pull Policy. If Not Present (pull only if the node lacks the image), Always (check the registry every time), Never (never pull; the image must already be on the node). Exam tip: An image tagged latest is pulled every time: for a local-only image set image Pull Policy to If Not Present or Never.

1.title: Using an image in a Pod, continued
1.text: Using an image in a Pod. The default is If Not Present, except when the tag is latest (or missing): then it is Always. That is why a local-only image tagged latest fails with err image pull: the kubelet insists on asking a registry that does not have it. Fix it by setting image Pull Policy If Not Present or Never, or use a real tag. image Pull Policy cannot be changed on a running Pod. Edit the yamel and recreate the Pod: kube control get pod p dash o yaml p dot yaml, change the field, then kube control replace the force flag dash f p dot yaml.

1.title: Using an image in a Pod, continued
1.text: Using an image in a Pod. Private registries. A Pod pulls from a private registry with image Pull Secrets, which names a Secret of type Kubernetes dot io slash dockerconfigjson (Module nine shows how to create Secrets). The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Container commands: ENTRYPOINT, CMD, command and args
1.text: Container commands: entry point, C M D, command and args. The Pod's container can replace what the image runs. entry point. Pod field: command. Effect: the program to run. C M D. Pod field: args. Effect: the arguments to the program. Exam tip: In a Pod, command replaces the image's entry point and args replaces its C M D.

1.title: Container commands: ENTRYPOINT, CMD, command and args, continued
1.text: Container commands: entry point, C M D, command and args. Rules: if you set command, the image's entry point and C M D are ignored; if you set only args, the image's entry point stays and args replaces C M D; if you set neither, the image's defaults run. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Container commands: ENTRYPOINT, CMD, command and args, continued
1.text: Container commands: entry point, C M D, command and args. On the command line, everything after -- is the command and arguments: kube control run job one the image flag set to busy box one dot thirty-six the restart flag set to Never then the command echo hello sets args to echo, hello (and keeps the image entry point, which is empty for busy box, so it still runs). Add the command flag to put it into command instead: kube control run job one the image flag set to busy box one dot thirty-six the restart flag set to Never the command flag then the command echo hello. Environment variables go in env ( name or value ) and are visible to the process: kube control run web the image flag set to engine X alpine the env flag set to mode prod. A value can also come from a Config Map or Secret (Module nine).

1.title: Container commands: ENTRYPOINT, CMD, command and args, continued
1.text: Container commands: entry point, C M D, command and args. Exam tip. The two most common image mistakes are the wrong tag (read the task twice) and latest with a local image. Verify with docker images (or pod man images ) after a build, and with kube control describe pod when a Pod will not start.

2.title: Lab 1.1: build image
2.text: Lab one point one: build image. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The directory about slash build slash hello contains a Docker file. Build an image from it and tag it hello one dot zero. (Use docker build; on an exam host that has pod man, the command is identical.). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.1: build image, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run cd about slash build slash hello. Then docker build dash t hello one dot zero. Then docker run the rm flag hello one dot zero. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.2: modify dockerfile
2.text: Lab one point two: modify dockerfile. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Docker file in about slash build slash greeter builds an image that prints hello. Modify the Docker file so that the image prints hello team and carries the label version two (it now has version one ), then build it and tag it greeter two dot zero. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.2: modify dockerfile, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run cd about slash build slash greeter. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then cat Docker file. Then docker build dash t greeter two dot zero. Then docker run the rm flag greeter two dot zero. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.3: save image archive
2.text: Lab one point three: save image archive. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. Build the image from the Docker file in about slash build slash hello, tag it hello three dot zero, and save it as an archive file about slash answers slash hello-three dot zero dot tar so that it can be loaded on another machine with docker load. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.3: save image archive, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run cd about slash build slash hello. Then docker build dash t hello three dot zero. Then docker save hello three dot zero about slash answers slash hello-three dot zero dot tar. Then tar -tf about slash answers slash hello-three dot zero dot tar then pipe to head. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.4: local image pull policy
2.text: Lab one point four: local image pull policy. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace local, the Pod localapp uses the image C K A D slash app latest. That image exists only in the local image store of the nodes (it is in no registry), and the Pod is stuck in err image pull or image pull back off. Fix it so the Pod is Running with the same image and the kubelet does not pull the image from a registry. Keep the Pod name and namespace. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.4: local image pull policy, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n local get pod localapp dash o yaml sed s slash image Pull Policy Always slash image Pull Policy If Not Present or slash temp slash localapp dot yaml. Then kube control replace the force flag dash f slash temp slash localapp dot yaml. Then kube control dash n local wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash localapp the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.5: command args
2.text: Lab one point five: command args. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace cmd, create a Pod named greeter with the image busy box one dot thirty-six that runs the program echo with the single argument Hello C K A D, using the command and args fields of the container (not a shell string). The Pod must not restart after it finishes ( restart Policy Never ). Wait until it has completed. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.5: command args, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n cmd run greeter the image flag set to busy box one dot thirty-six the restart flag set to Never the dry run flag set to client dash o yaml slash, and so on. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then kube control apply dash f slash temp slash greeter dot yaml. Then kube control dash n cmd wait the for flag set to json path dot status dot phase Succeeded pod slash greeter the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n cmd logs greeter. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which Docker file line sets the base image? Answer: from. Question two. Which command builds an image from the Docker file in the current folder and tags it hello one dot zero? Answer: docker build dash t hello one dot zero. (or pod man build dash t hello one dot zero. ). Question three. How do you save an image to a file, and how do you load it again? Answer: docker save hello one dot zero hello dot tar and docker load hello dot tar (pod man: pod man save dash o, pod man load dash i ).

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is the default image Pull Policy for an image tagged latest? Answer: Always; for any other tag it is If Not Present. Question five. Which Pod field replaces the image's entry point, and which replaces its C M D? Answer: command replaces entry point; args replaces C M D. Question six. What does expose eighty eighty do? Answer: It documents the port; it does not publish or open it.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. Can you edit image Pull Policy on a running Pod? Answer: No; export the yamel, change it and recreate the Pod ( kube control replace the force flag dash f ). Question eight. Why use a multi-stage build? Answer: To copy only the build result into a small final image without the build tools.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Docker file: from, run, copy, environment, label, expose, user, entry point, C M D. Build: docker build dash t name tag.; pod man is identical. Save and load: docker save name tag f dot tar; docker load f dot tar. Pull policy: default If Not Present; latest means Always; Never for local-only images. Command and args: command equals entry point, args equals C M D; -- on kube control run. Private registry: image Pull Secrets with a docker registry Secret. Immutable: image Pull Policy cannot change in place: replace the force flag. If this course is helping you, please subscribe to the channel and hit the bell icon, so you get a notification when the next video is out. In the next module, we continue the course.
